content: The recommendations provided update the information on vaccines and antiviral agents available for controlling influenza during the 1992-1993 influenza season, replacing the previous guidelines from 1991. Influenza A viruses are classified into subtypes based on two surface antigens: hemagglutinin (H) and neuraminidase (N). Among these, three hemagglutinin subtypes (H1, H2, H3) and two neuraminidase subtypes (N1, N2) have been identified as causing widespread human disease. Immunity to these antigens, particularly hemagglutinin, reduces the likelihood of infection and mitigates disease severity if infection occurs. However, infection with one subtype provides little or no protection against other subtypes. Additionally, antigenic drift within a subtype can result in significant variation, such that immunity from infection or vaccination with one strain may not protect against distantly related strains of the same subtype. Influenza B viruses exhibit greater antigenic stability than Influenza A viruses, but antigenic variation still occurs. Consequently, major epidemics of respiratory disease caused by new influenza variants continue to emerge. The antigenic characteristics of currently circulating strains guide the selection of virus strains included in each year’s vaccine. Typical influenza illness is marked by the sudden onset of fever, muscle aches, sore throat, and a nonproductive cough. Unlike other common respiratory infections, influenza can cause severe malaise lasting several days. More severe illness may occur if primary influenza pneumonia or secondary bacterial pneumonia develops. During influenza epidemics, high attack rates of acute illness lead to increased visits to physicians, clinics, and emergency rooms, as well as higher hospitalization rates for managing lower respiratory tract complications. Elderly individuals and those with underlying health conditions are at increased risk for complications from influenza infection. If infected, these high-risk groups are more likely to require hospitalization compared to the general population. During major epidemics, hospitalization rates for high-risk individuals may increase twoto fivefold, depending on the age group. Previously healthy children and younger adults may also require hospitalization for influenza-related complications, but their relative increase in hospitalization rates is lower than that of high-risk groups. Increased mortality during influenza epidemics highlights the impact of the disease. Mortality rises not only from influenza and pneumonia but also from exacerbations of cardiopulmonary and other chronic diseases triggered by influenza infection. For example, during epidemics between 1977 and 1988, more than 40,000 excess deaths occurred during two of these epidemics, with 80%-90% of deaths attributed to pneumonia and influenza occurring among individuals aged 65 years or older. As the population ages and chronic diseases associated with aging become more prevalent, the burden of influenza is expected to increase unless control measures are implemented more rigorously. The number of younger individuals at increased risk for influenza-related complications is also rising due to advances in neonatal intensive care, improved management of diseases like cystic fibrosis and AIDS, and better survival rates for organ transplant recipients. Annual vaccination of high-risk individuals before the influenza season is the most effective strategy for reducing the impact of influenza. Vaccination is highly cost-effective when targeted at individuals most likely to experience complications or those at increased risk of exposure. Administering the vaccine to high-risk individuals during routine healthcare visits or hospitalizations before the influenza season eliminates the need for special visits to clinics. Recent studies indicate that when vaccine and epidemic strains are well-matched, achieving high vaccination rates in closed populations can reduce the risk of outbreaks by inducing herd immunity. Vaccination is also recommended for individuals who wish to avoid influenza infection, reduce disease severity, or minimize the risk of transmitting influenza to high-risk individuals with whom they have frequent contact. The antiviral agent amantadine hydrochloride is effective only against Influenza A and must be administered throughout the period of risk for maximum prophylactic effectiveness. When used as prophylaxis or therapy, the potential effectiveness of amantadine must be weighed against possible side effects. Chemoprophylaxis is not a substitute for vaccination. Recommendations for chemoprophylaxis are primarily intended to assist healthcare providers in making decisions for individuals at the greatest risk of severe illness and complications if infected with Influenza A. Amantadine is also approved for use by anyone wishing to reduce their chances of becoming ill with Influenza A. The inactivated influenza vaccine is made from highly purified, egg-grown viruses rendered noninfectious. It cannot cause influenza. Each year’s vaccine contains three virus strains (usually two type A and one type B) believed likely to circulate in the upcoming winter. The vaccine composition is designed to minimize systemic or febrile reactions. Subvirion or purified-surface-antigen preparations are recommended for children to reduce febrile reactions, while any preparation may be used for adults. Most vaccinated children and young adults develop high post-vaccination hemagglutination-inhibition antibody titers, which protect against infection by strains similar to those in the vaccine or related variants that may emerge during outbreaks. Elderly individuals and those with certain chronic diseases may develop lower post-vaccination antibody titers than healthy young adults, leaving them susceptible to upper respiratory tract infections. However, even if such individuals develop influenza illness, the vaccine has been shown to prevent lower respiratory tract involvement and other complications, reducing the risk of hospitalization and death. Influenza vaccination is strongly recommended for individuals aged six months or older who are at increased risk for influenza complications due to age or underlying medical conditions. Healthcare workers and others in close contact with high-risk individuals should also be vaccinated. Additionally, vaccination may be administered to anyone wishing to reduce their risk of influenza infection. The trivalent influenza vaccine for the 1992-1993 season includes A/Texas/36/91-like (H1N1), A/Beijing/353/89-like (H3N2), and B/Panama/45/90-like hemagglutinin antigens. Annual vaccination is necessary because immunity declines within a year. Supplies of the previous season’s vaccine should not be used for the current season. Two doses administered at least one month apart may be required for satisfactory antibody response in previously unvaccinated children under nine years of age. However, studies have shown little or no improvement in antibody responses when a second dose is administered to adults during the same season. Data on influenza vaccine immunogenicity and side effects have been obtained from intramuscular administration. The intramuscular route is recommended due to the lack of adequate evaluation of other routes. Adults and older children should be vaccinated in the deltoid muscle, while infants and young children should be vaccinated in the anterolateral aspect of the thigh. To maximize protection for high-risk individuals, they and their close contacts should be targeted for organized vaccination programs. High-risk groups include individuals aged 65 years or older, residents of nursing homes and chronic-care facilities, individuals with chronic pulmonary or cardiovascular disorders, and children and teenagers receiving long-term aspirin therapy. Healthcare workers and household members in close contact with high-risk individuals should also be vaccinated to reduce the risk of transmitting influenza. Pregnant women with medical conditions that increase their risk of influenza complications should be vaccinated, as the vaccine is considered safe during pregnancy. Vaccination after the first trimester is a reasonable precaution to minimize theoretical risks of teratogenicity. However, vaccination should not be delayed for high-risk pregnant women who will still be in their first trimester when the influenza season begins. For individuals infected with HIV, vaccination is a prudent precaution, as influenza may result in serious illness and complications. However, antibody responses to the vaccine may be lower in individuals with advanced HIV-related illnesses, and booster doses have not improved immune responses in these cases. Foreign travelers, particularly those at high risk, should review their vaccination history and consider vaccination before travel to regions where influenza activity is expected. High-risk individuals vaccinated with the previous season’s vaccine should be revaccinated with the current vaccine upon returning. Inactivated influenza vaccine should not be administered to individuals with anaphylactic hypersensitivity to eggs or other vaccine components without consulting a physician. Amantadine hydrochloride may be an option for preventing Influenza A in such individuals. Vaccination should be delayed for adults with acute febrile illnesses until symptoms subside, but minor illnesses should not contraindicate vaccination. The most common side effect of vaccination is soreness at the injection site, lasting up to two days. Rarely, immediate allergic reactions may occur, likely due to residual egg protein. Individuals with severe egg allergies should consult a physician for evaluation before vaccination.
